genZNote: The reason 'clean-looking' lake water and fish tanks aren't automatically safe for open wounds — it's an oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod that thrives in fresh water.

morphology.motility: Motile via a single polar flagellum

habitat.naturalHabitat: Fresh and brackish water, sediment, and moist soil worldwide
habitat.hostAssociation: Environmental organism; opportunistic pathogen of humans, fish, and amphibians
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Common in lakes, rivers, ponds, and even chlorinated water systems and aquariums

culture.media: Blood agar, MacConkey agar; selective Aeromonas media available
culture.growthCharacteristics: Facultative anaerobe, grows well at a wide temperature range (4-42°C)
culture.colonyMorphology: Large, smooth, often beta-hemolytic colonies on blood agar

identificationClues: Oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod, an important distinguishing feature from the oxidase-negative Enterobacterales it otherwise resembles biochemically
Classic exposure history involves freshwater contact — swimming, fishing injuries, leech therapy, or contaminated wounds near lakes/rivers
Can cause both wound infections and self-limited to severe gastroenteritis

diseases: Wound and soft-tissue infections (often after freshwater exposure)
Cellulitis, sometimes progressing to necrotizing fasciitis in immunocompromised hosts
clinicalImportance.transmission: Freshwater/brackish water exposure to wounds, ingestion of contaminated water or food, medicinal leech therapy
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: A well-known cause of infection after freshwater trauma (e.g., fishing hook injuries, near-drowning) and after medicinal leech use
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Oxidase positivity distinguishes it from morphologically similar Enterobacterales on routine biochemical panels

examFacts.importantTest: Oxidase test; exposure history to fresh/brackish water
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod strongly linked to freshwater exposure and medicinal leech therapy
